intro: Every sport needs a room and someone in charge of it. In the late 1800s and early 1900s, American cities built many kinds of sports rooms. There were boxing clubs, YMCA gyms, settlement house gyms, park field houses, ballrooms and school gyms. Each room had its own owners, its own rules and its own crowd.

This unit follows two sports through those rooms. Boxing moved from secret fields to licensed arenas, and newspapers and radio made its fights national news. Yet Illinois school leagues never took it in. Basketball began in a YMCA in 1891 and spread through Ys, settlement houses, parks, ballrooms and school tournaments. Along the way, many people were shut out by race or sex, and you will learn the dates when doors opened.

By the end, you will be able to name the groups that ran each room, from the YMCA and Hull-House to the IHSA and state athletic commissions. You will be able to explain why a fight could fill the front page while the school board said no. You will also be able to trace Chicago's part in this story with real dates.
bigQuestion: Who decided which games belonged in the school gym, and which stayed in the club, the park and the newspaper?

chapters.title: Boxing and the Newspaper
chapters.bigQuestion: Why did boxing fill the front page but stay out of the school gym?

story.title: A Headline on the Front Step
story.kicker: A Chicago boy reads about a giant fight his own school would never host.
paragraphs: Chicago, September 1927. A boy named Leo sits on the front step of a two-flat on the West Side. His father's newspaper is spread across his knees. The biggest headline is about a fight. Jack Dempsey will meet Gene Tunney at Soldier Field in a few days.

The paper prints both boxers' weights and their records. It lists ticket prices and the streetcar lines that run to the lakefront. Leo counts the columns. The fight takes up more space than the baseball scores do.

Leo's high school has a basketball team and a track team. They play other schools under the rules of the state high school association. There is no boxing team. The school gym is for classes and games, not for prizefights.

Down the street, a club above a hardware store has a ring. Men and older boys box there at night. The club does not answer to the school board. It answers to its owners, and sometimes to the state boxing board.

On fight night, September 22, Leo has no ticket. He listens with his neighbors around a radio in the corner store. A voice from Soldier Field fills the room. The whole block hears the same fight at the same moment.
story.think: Why might a newspaper sell a fight that a school would not host?

lessons.title: Boxing at Ancient Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: Boxing joined the ancient Olympic Games in 688 BCE, long before any modern rule book.
reading: Ancient Greeks held games at *Olympia*, a holy site in southern Greece, to honor the god Zeus. The first recorded Olympic Games there are dated to 776 BCE. Later Greek writers say boxing was added in 688 BCE. Winners went home to their cities as heroes. Some cities put up statues of them.

Greek boxers wrapped their hands in leather straps called *himantes*. There were no weight classes, so a small man could face a much larger one. There were no timed rounds either. A bout went on until one boxer gave up or could not go on.

Vase painters showed boxers on pottery, and many of those pots survive in museums today. The ancient games are usually said to have ended in the late 300s CE. Much later, in the 1700s, fights for money grew popular in England. Those fights needed new rules, and the people who hosted them wrote the rules.

words.d: a holy site in southern Greece where the ancient Olympic Games were held
leather straps that ancient Greek boxers wrapped around their hands

look.title: A Scene on a Greek Vase
look.text: Many Greek vases from the 500s BCE show boxing. A common scene: two bearded athletes face each other. Leather straps wind around their hands. Beside them stands an official holding a long stick. Greek games used officials like this to keep order and punish rule breakers.
look.prompt: What does the official with the stick tell you about how the Greeks ran their games?

check.q: When do Greek writers say boxing was added to the ancient Olympic Games?
check.why: Later Greek writers date boxing at Olympia to 688 BCE; 776 BCE is the date of the first recorded games.

check.q: What were himantes?
choices: leather straps wrapped around a boxer's hands
check.why: Himantes were the leather hand straps of ancient Greek boxers.

check.q: Which was true of ancient Greek boxing?
choices: A bout went on until one boxer gave up or could not go on.
check.why: Greek boxing had no weight classes and no timed rounds; a bout ended when one boxer gave up or could not continue.

lessons.title: Broughton's Rules, 1743
lessons.mainIdea: In 1743 Jack Broughton wrote the oldest known set of boxing rules for fights in his London building.
reading: In the 1700s, crowds in London paid to watch fights for money. A fight for a cash prize was called a *prizefight*. One of the best-known fighters was Jack Broughton. In 1743 he opened his own *amphitheater* in London. An amphitheater is a building with rising rows of seats around a stage.

Broughton posted seven rules for fights in his building. They are the oldest known written rules for boxing. Historians call them *Broughton's Rules*. One rule gave a fallen man half a minute to return to the middle of the stage. Another barred hitting a man who was down.

The rules also said that umpires would settle arguments and that the prize money would be split. Broughton's Rules were used for nearly a hundred years. In 1838 new rules replaced them, called the London Prize Ring Rules. Both codes were written for fights with bare fists.

words.d: a fight held for a cash prize, often with paying spectators
a building with rising rows of seats around a central stage
seven rules for boxing posted by Jack Broughton in London in 1743

look.title: From Broughton's Rules
look.text: A man who is down must not be struck. If he cannot come back to the middle of the stage within half a minute, he is judged beaten. Umpires chosen by the two sides settle any dispute.
look.cite: Jack Broughton, rules for his amphitheater, London, 1743
look.prompt: Which rule protects a fighter who has fallen, and who settles arguments?

check.q: Who wrote the oldest known boxing rules in 1743?
check.why: Jack Broughton posted his seven rules in London in 1743.

check.q: What is a prizefight?
choices: a fight held for a cash prize

check.why: A prizefight is a fight held for money, often in front of paying spectators.

check.q: What replaced Broughton's Rules in 1838?
check.why: The London Prize Ring Rules of 1838 replaced Broughton's code for bare-fist fights.

lessons.title: The Queensberry Rules, 1867
lessons.mainIdea: The Queensberry Rules of 1867 required gloves and three-minute rounds, and modern boxing rules grew from them.
reading: In 1867 a new set of boxing rules appeared in Britain. A Welsh sportsman named John Graham Chambers wrote them. The Marquess of Queensberry, a Scottish nobleman, lent his name as a sponsor. So the code became known as the *Queensberry Rules*.

The new rules required gloves. They set each *round*, a timed part of a bout, at three minutes, with one minute of rest between rounds. A fighter who went down had ten seconds to get up. Wrestling holds were not allowed. A bare-fist contest with no clock became a timed contest with a count.

At first, many professional fights still used the older London Prize Ring Rules. Fights with no gloves were called *bare-knuckle* fights. By the 1890s, championship bouts had moved to the Queensberry Rules. Amateur clubs used them too. Most boxing rule books around the world still grow from this 1867 code.

words.d: boxing rules published in 1867 that required gloves and three-minute rounds
a timed part of a boxing bout, followed by a short rest
fought with bare fists, without gloves

check.why: John Graham Chambers wrote the rules; the Marquess of Queensberry lent his name as sponsor.

check.q: What was new about the Queensberry Rules compared with the London Prize Ring Rules?

lessons.title: Secret Fights in America
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s prizefighting was against the law in most U.S. states, so big fights were held in hidden places.
reading: In the 1800s most American states banned prizefighting. Lawmakers and church leaders saw it as brutal and tied to gambling. Fights still happened anyway. A *promoter* is a person who organizes a fight and sells it to the public. Promoters picked hidden spots and moved crowds by train or boat, often at the last minute.

The most famous illegal fight took place on July 8, 1889, near Richburg, Mississippi. John L. Sullivan, the *heavyweight* champion, met Jake Kilrain. They fought bare-knuckle under the London Prize Ring Rules. The fight lasted 75 rounds in the summer heat, and Sullivan won.

It was the last heavyweight title fight held with bare fists. Mississippi's governor had tried to stop it, and both fighters faced legal trouble afterward. The case showed a gap between the law and the public. Thousands of people wanted to watch, and newspapers across the country printed the result.

words.d: a person who organizes a sports event and sells it to the public
the heaviest weight class in boxing; its champion was the most famous title holder

check.why: The 1889 fight was bare-knuckle under the London Prize Ring Rules.

lessons.title: Gloves in New Orleans, 1892
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892 James J. Corbett beat John L. Sullivan in a gloved title fight in New Orleans, but Sullivan had kept Black boxers out.
reading: New Orleans allowed glove contests at *athletic clubs*, private clubs that hosted sports for members and paying guests. In September 1892 the Olympic Club of New Orleans held three nights of title fights. On September 7, Sullivan fought James J. Corbett, a former bank clerk from San Francisco. They wore gloves and fought under the Queensberry Rules.

Corbett won in the 21st round. He became the first heavyweight champion crowned under the Queensberry Rules. Telegraph wires carried the result across the country that night. The fight helped end the bare-knuckle era at the top of the sport.

Sullivan had also drawn a *color line*. He said he would not fight a Black challenger. That shut out Peter Jackson, a Black boxer born in the Danish West Indies who fought out of Australia. Many writers of the time rated Jackson among the best heavyweights alive. He never got a title fight against Sullivan.

words.d: a private club that hosted sports for its members and paying guests
a rule or custom that kept Black athletes out of a sport, team or title fight

lessons.title: State Boards Take Charge
lessons.mainIdea: Starting in the late 1890s, some states made boxing legal again under state rules and athletic commissions.
reading: Some states chose to control boxing instead of banning it. Nevada made prizefighting legal in 1897. That let James J. Corbett and Bob Fitzsimmons fight in Carson City on March 17, 1897. A camera crew filmed the bout, and the film was shown in theaters in many cities.

New York passed the Walker Law in 1920. It was named for state senator James J. Walker, who later became mayor of New York City. The law created the New York State Athletic Commission. An *athletic commission* is a state board that licenses boxers, referees and promoters. It can suspend anyone who breaks its rules.

Other states followed with boards of their own. Illinois allowed licensed professional boxing again in the 1920s. That opened the door for huge fights in Chicago stadiums and ballparks. A *license* is official permission from the government to do a job. With licenses, a state could check fighters, set rules and collect taxes on tickets.

words.d: a state board that licenses boxers, referees and promoters and enforces rules
official permission from the government to do a job or hold an event

look.title: A Boxer's License Card
look.text: Picture a small card from the 1920s. It shows a photograph, a name, a home city and a weight. A state seal is stamped in one corner. A commissioner has signed it. The card must be shown before the boxer may enter the ring.
look.prompt: What can a state do with a license system that it could not do with a ban?

check.why: Nevada legalized prizefighting in 1897, allowing the Corbett and Fitzsimmons fight in Carson City.

check.q: What did New York's Walker Law of 1920 create?
choices: the New York State Athletic Commission
check.why: The Walker Law set up a state commission to license and control boxing.

choices: a state board that licenses boxers and enforces rules

lessons.title: Boxing Sells Papers
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1800s and early 1900s, newspapers and magazines turned boxing into a public story that sold copies.
reading: Big city newspapers began printing a regular *sports section* in the 1880s and 1890s. Editors learned that sports news sold papers. Boxing was a favorite subject. A title fight gave writers weeks of stories before the bout and days of stories after it.

The National Police Gazette led the way. Richard K. Fox owned it from the late 1870s. The magazine was printed on pink paper and was read in barbershops and saloons. Fox handed out championship belts and offered prize money. His paper helped build the idea of one national champion in each weight class.

In 1922 Nat Fleischer started The Ring magazine in New York. The Ring ranked boxers and printed the results of their fights. A boxer's *record* is the written list of his wins and losses. Fans, writers and promoters used those lists to argue over who deserved a title fight.

words.d: the part of a newspaper that reports on games and athletes
the written list of an athlete's wins and losses

look.title: A Pink Magazine in a Barbershop
look.text: Picture a barbershop in 1885. Men wait their turn on a bench. A pink magazine lies on the counter. It prints drawings of boxers, a challenge from one fighter to another and an offer of a championship belt from the owner of the magazine.
look.prompt: How could a magazine owner shape who was called champion?

check.why: Richard K. Fox owned the Police Gazette and used it to promote boxing.

check.q: What did The Ring magazine, started in 1922, do?
choices: It ranked boxers and printed fight results.
It licensed promoters in New York.
check.why: Nat Fleischer's The Ring ranked boxers and kept fight records.

check.q: Why did newspaper editors give boxing so much space?
choices: Sports news, and boxing especially, sold papers.
check.why: Editors found that sports stories sold copies, and title fights gave weeks of news.

lessons.title: Jack Johnson's Title
lessons.mainIdea: In 1908 Jack Johnson became the first Black heavyweight champion, and many white Americans answered with violence and new laws.
reading: Jack Johnson was born in Galveston, Texas, in 1878. For years white champions refused to fight him. On December 26, 1908, he finally met champion Tommy Burns in Sydney, Australia. Johnson won. He became the first Black world heavyweight champion.

Many white writers called for a *Great White Hope* to beat him. Former champion James J. Jeffries came out of retirement. They fought on July 4, 1910, in Reno, Nevada, and Johnson won. That night, white mobs attacked Black people in many American cities, and people were killed.

Films of the Reno fight showed a Black man beating a white man. In 1912 Congress passed a law banning the shipment of prizefight films across state lines. That same year Johnson, who lived in Chicago, opened a nightclub there called the Café de Champion. In 1913 he was convicted under the Mann Act, in a case many historians describe as racially motivated.

Johnson left the country rather than go to prison. He lost his title to Jess Willard in Havana, Cuba, in 1915. No Black boxer held the heavyweight title again until 1937. In 2018 President Donald Trump granted Johnson a *pardon*, an official act of forgiveness, 72 years after his death.

words.d: a phrase used in the 1910s for a white boxer who might beat Jack Johnson
an official act by a president or governor that forgives a crime

look.cite: Geoffrey C. Ward, Unforgivable Blackness: The Rise and Fall of Jack Johnson (2004); presidential pardon, 2018

check.q: Where did Jack Johnson win the heavyweight title in 1908?
check.why: Johnson beat Tommy Burns in Sydney on December 26, 1908.

check.q: What happened after Johnson beat Jeffries on July 4, 1910?
choices: White mobs attacked Black people in many cities.
check.why: The Reno fight was followed by racist violence in many American cities.

check.q: What did the federal law of 1912 ban?
choices: all boxing in the United States

check.why: In 1912 Congress banned moving prizefight films between states, after the Reno fight film.

lessons.title: Radio at Ringside
lessons.mainIdea: Radio in the 1920s and 1930s let millions follow a fight live, and two of the biggest fights of that era were held in Chicago.
reading: On July 2, 1921, Jack Dempsey fought Georges Carpentier of France in Jersey City, New Jersey. The arena was a wooden bowl built for the fight, called Boyle's Thirty Acres. Promoter Tex Rickard organized it. Ticket sales passed one million dollars, the first million-dollar *gate* in boxing. A gate is the money taken in from tickets.

The fight was also carried by radio, then a brand-new technology. People gathered in halls and theaters to hear reports from ringside. It was one of the first big sports events on the air. A *broadcast* is a program sent out over the air for anyone with a receiver to hear.

On September 22, 1927, Dempsey fought Gene Tunney at Soldier Field in Chicago before more than 100,000 people. Graham McNamee described it on NBC radio. When Tunney went down in the seventh round, the count was delayed. A rule required the standing boxer to go to a neutral corner first. Tunney won, and the bout is still called the Long Count fight.

On June 22, 1937, Joe Louis beat James J. Braddock at Comiskey Park in Chicago. Louis became the first Black heavyweight champion since Jack Johnson. Radio carried his fights into homes across the country. In 1938 his rematch with Max Schmeling of Germany became a symbol in the years before World War II.

words.d: the total money taken in from ticket sales for an event
a program sent out over the air by radio or television

look.title: One Voice, Many Rooms
look.text: September 22, 1927. More than 100,000 people sit in Soldier Field. Across the country, many more sit in kitchens, stores and halls around radio sets. They cannot see the ring. They hear one announcer's voice describe each round as it happens.
look.prompt: How did radio change who could be part of a big fight?

choices: It was the first fight with gloves.
It was the first million-dollar gate in boxing.

check.why: Tex Rickard's 1921 fight in Jersey City took in more than one million dollars in tickets.

check.why: Dempsey and Tunney fought at Soldier Field on September 22, 1927.

check.q: Where did Joe Louis win the heavyweight title in 1937?
check.why: Louis beat James J. Braddock at Comiskey Park on June 22, 1937.

lessons.title: Golden Gloves and the CYO
lessons.mainIdea: Amateur boxing grew in city programs run by newspapers and churches, outside school leagues.
reading: An *amateur* is an athlete who competes without being paid. In the 1920s, big newspapers began running amateur boxing tournaments called the *Golden Gloves*. The New York Daily News held one in New York. The Chicago Tribune held one in Chicago, pushed by its sports editor, Arch Ward. Champions from the two cities later met in intercity bouts.

The newspapers printed the brackets, the names and the results. A tournament gave a paper weeks of stories to sell. Young boxers from factory towns and city blocks could see their names in print. Golden Gloves finals in Chicago filled large arenas.

In 1930 Bishop Bernard Sheil founded the *Catholic Youth Organization*, or CYO, in Chicago. Boxing became one of its best-known programs. Parish halls and city arenas hosted CYO bouts. Sheil welcomed boys of different races and religions, at a time when many Chicago spaces were segregated.

words.d: an athlete who competes without being paid
amateur boxing tournaments begun by newspapers in the 1920s
a youth program founded in Chicago in 1930 by Bishop Bernard Sheil; known as the CYO

lessons.title: Why School Leagues Chose Wrestling
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois school sport crowned wrestling champions from 1937 but never boxing ones, and college boxing ended after a death in 1960.
reading: The *IHSA*, the Illinois High School Association, dates from 1900. It sets rules for school sports and runs state tournaments. Over the years it added basketball, track and many other sports. Boxing never became one of its state championship sports. Boxing stayed in clubs, parks, churches and newspaper tournaments.

Wrestling took a different path. Many school leaders saw it as safer for students than boxing. The IHSA crowned its first boys wrestling state champions in 1937. Girls wrestling got its own IHSA state finals in the 2021–22 season, with the first champions crowned in 2022.

Colleges did hold boxing for a time. The *NCAA*, which runs college sports, held a national boxing championship starting in 1932. In April 1960, Charlie Mohr of the University of Wisconsin collapsed after a bout at the NCAA tournament and died days later. Wisconsin dropped boxing, and the NCAA held no boxing championship after 1960.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900, which runs state tournaments for Illinois schools
the National Collegiate Athletic Association, which runs college sports in the United States

check.why: The IHSA crowned its first boys wrestling champions in 1937; it never held boxing championships.

check.why: The first IHSA girls wrestling state finals came in the 2021–22 season.

lessons.title: Women Enter the Ring
lessons.mainIdea: Women were long barred from organized amateur boxing; a 1993 court case and the 2012 Olympics opened the door.
reading: For most of its history, organized boxing shut women out. Some women boxed in shows and exhibitions, but most commissions would not license them. *USA Boxing*, the body that runs amateur boxing in the United States, did not allow women to compete for decades.

In 1993 a 16-year-old named Dallas Malloy of Washington State sued USA Boxing. A federal judge ruled against the ban, and USA Boxing changed its rules. That October, Malloy fought in the first *sanctioned* women's amateur bout in the country. Sanctioned means approved by the official governing body.

Men's boxing had been part of the modern Olympics since 1904 in St. Louis. Women's boxing entered the Olympic Games in London in 2012, with three weight classes. Claressa Shields, a 17-year-old from Flint, Michigan, won the middleweight gold medal. She won gold again in Rio de Janeiro in 2016.

words.d: the organization that governs amateur boxing in the United States
approved by the official governing body of a sport

look.title: A Rule and a Lawsuit
look.text: Before 1993: an amateur rule book lets only males enter sanctioned bouts. A 16-year-old girl has trained for years. She asks a federal court whether the rule is fair. The judge rules for her, and the governing body rewrites its rule book.

chapters.title: Basketball in the Neighborhood
chapters.bigQuestion: Which city rooms gave basketball a home before television, and who ran them?

story.title: The Net in the Alley
story.kicker: One hoop behind a garage, and four different courts nearby.
paragraphs: Chicago's South Side, the 1950s. A metal hoop is bolted above a garage door behind a row of houses. Someone has hung a chain net from the rim. It rattles each time the ball drops through. In the morning the alley is a road for trash trucks. After school it is a court.

No league owns this court. No referee comes. The players are neighbors, and they settle their own arguments. Down the block, the park field house has a wooden floor, a glass backboard and a director who keeps a schedule on a clipboard.

On Saturdays some of the boys go to the YMCA on Wabash Avenue. It has a gym and a pool. It was built for Black Chicagoans, who were turned away from many other Ys. Some of their fathers played in that same gym as boys.

On Friday night the older kids crowd into the high school gym to watch the school team. A few families own television sets now, but most basketball still happens in rooms like these. The alley, the field house, the Y and the school gym each have their own rules and their own keepers.
story.think: Who made the rules in each of these four rooms, and who could come in?

lessons.title: A Game Built for the YMCA
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball was invented in 1891 at a YMCA training school, and the YMCA's network carried it to other cities.
reading: The *YMCA*, or Young Men's Christian Association, began in London in 1844. George Williams founded it for young men who worked in the city's shops. The first American YMCA opened in Boston in 1851. By the late 1800s, many YMCA buildings in American cities had a *gymnasium*, a large room for exercise and games.

In Springfield, Massachusetts, the YMCA ran a school that trained its future leaders. Luther Gulick directed its physical education work. In late 1891 he asked instructor James Naismith to invent an indoor game for the winter months. Naismith wrote 13 rules and used peach baskets as goals.

The rules were printed in the school's paper, The Triangle, in January 1892. Graduates of the school took jobs at YMCAs in other cities. Each one could carry the game to a new gym. Within a few years, YMCAs across the United States and in other countries were playing basketball.

words.d: the Young Men's Christian Association, founded in London in 1844, known for city gyms
a large indoor room for exercise and games; often shortened to gym

look.title: Naismith Remembers the Assignment
look.text: Naismith later wrote that his class of young men was restless in winter. Marching and exercises bored them. He was asked to find a game that could be played indoors, in a gym, and would hold their interest.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development, 1941
look.prompt: What problem was the new game meant to solve for the YMCA school?

check.q: Where and when was the YMCA founded?
check.why: George Williams founded the YMCA in London in 1844; the first American Y opened in Boston in 1851.

check.q: Who asked James Naismith to invent an indoor game?
check.why: Luther Gulick, who led physical education at the Springfield school, gave Naismith the task.

check.q: How did basketball spread so fast in the 1890s?
choices: YMCA graduates carried it to Ys in other cities.
The NBA sent teams on tour.
check.why: The YMCA's network of trained leaders took the new game to gyms across the country.

lessons.title: Too Crowded for the Y
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball grew so popular that some YMCAs limited it, and players moved to rented halls and paid teams.
reading: Basketball filled YMCA gyms fast. A single game could take over a floor that many members wanted for exercise classes. In the 1890s some YMCAs limited basketball or pushed teams out. The players looked for other rooms.

Teams rented *armories*, lodge halls and dance halls. An armory is a large building where a state's militia kept its equipment and drilled. Teams charged admission to pay the rent. In 1896 a team in Trenton, New Jersey, paid its players, in one of the earliest known professional games. A *professional* is an athlete who is paid to play.

Rented halls brought new problems. Fans in balconies reached out and knocked the ball away. A *backboard*, first added in the mid-1890s, blocked them. Some early professional games were played inside a wire or rope cage around the floor. That is why basketball players were once nicknamed cagers.

words.d: large buildings where a state's militia stored equipment; many were rented for games and dances
an athlete who is paid to play
the board behind the basket, first added in the 1890s partly to stop balcony fans from reaching the ball

lessons.title: The Wabash Avenue YMCA
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Wabash Avenue YMCA opened in 1913 so Black Chicagoans, shut out of many Ys, had a Y of their own.
reading: In the early 1900s many YMCAs in the United States were *segregated*. That means Black people were kept out or sent to separate buildings. In 1910 Julius Rosenwald, a leader of Sears, Roebuck and Company in Chicago, made an offer. He would give $25,000 toward a YMCA for Black residents in any city that raised $75,000 more.

Chicago raised the money. The Wabash Avenue YMCA opened in 1913 at 3763 South Wabash Avenue, in the neighborhood later called Bronzeville. It had a gym, a pool and rooms for men new to the city. Many came north in the *Great Migration*, when millions of Black Southerners moved to Northern cities.

The building was more than a gym. In 1915 historian Carter G. Woodson and others founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History there. That group started Negro History Week in 1926, which grew into Black History Month. The building is now a Chicago landmark.

words.d: separated by race, with Black people kept out or sent to separate places
the movement of millions of Black Southerners to Northern and Western cities in the 1900s

lessons.title: Henderson's Courts in Washington
lessons.mainIdea: Edwin Bancroft Henderson brought organized basketball to Black students in Washington, D.C., starting in 1904.
reading: Edwin Bancroft Henderson was a Black physical education teacher in Washington, D.C. In the summer of 1904 he took classes at Harvard University and learned basketball there. He came home and began teaching it to Black students in the city's segregated schools. Black students were not allowed on many of the city's white teams and courts.

Henderson helped build *leagues*, groups of teams that play each other on a schedule. In 1906 he helped found the Interscholastic Athletic Association of Middle Atlantic States. *Interscholastic* means between schools. The association organized sports for Black schools in the region.

Henderson also wrote history. His 1939 book, The Negro in Sports, recorded the records of Black athletes that many newspapers ignored. In 2013 he was elected to the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame as a contributor. Many historians call him the father of Black basketball.

words.d: groups of teams that play one another on a set schedule
between schools, such as games played by one school against another

look.title: Why Henderson Wrote It Down

check.why: Henderson took summer classes at Harvard in 1904 and learned the game there.

check.why: Interscholastic means between schools, as in Henderson's 1906 association.

lessons.title: Hull-House Opens Its Doors
lessons.mainIdea: Hull-House, opened in Chicago in 1889, gave immigrant neighbors classes, clubs and a gym.
reading: In 1889 Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened *Hull-House* on Halsted Street in Chicago. It was a *settlement house*: educated people lived in a poor neighborhood and ran classes and clubs for their neighbors. The idea came from Toynbee Hall, which opened in London in 1884. Addams had visited it.

Many Hull-House neighbors were *immigrants*, people who had moved from another country. They came from Italy, Greece, Russia, Ireland, Germany and other places. Many families lived in crowded buildings with no yard. Hull-House grew into a group of buildings that included a gymnasium for clubs, classes and games.

Settlement leaders believed clubs and games taught young people to work together. Lillian Wald opened the Henry Street Settlement in New York in 1893. In 1931 Jane Addams became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Her work made Chicago a center of the settlement movement.

words.d: the settlement house Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened in Chicago in 1889
a neighborhood center where reformers lived and ran classes and clubs for their neighbors
people who move to a new country to live

look.prompt: What does this schedule tell you about who the gym was for and what the settlement wanted?

choices: a neighborhood center where reformers lived and ran classes and clubs
check.why: Settlement workers lived in the neighborhood and ran programs for their neighbors.

lessons.title: Field Houses in Chicago Parks
lessons.mainIdea: In 1905 Chicago opened neighborhood parks with field houses, giving crowded blocks indoor gyms of their own.
reading: In 1869 the Illinois legislature created three park boards for Chicago: the South, West and Lincoln Park commissions. Their first parks were large and far from the most crowded neighborhoods. Children in *tenements*, crowded apartment buildings, had few places to play. Reformers pushed for small parks close to home.

In 1905 the South Park Commission opened ten new neighborhood parks. Each had a *field house*, a building with a gym, showers, clubrooms and often a branch library. The Olmsted Brothers landscape firm and the architects of D. H. Burnham and Company designed them. Park leaders from other cities came to study them.

In 1934 the city's many separate park boards merged into one, the *Chicago Park District*. Twenty-two districts joined. Field houses became the gyms of the neighborhoods. Park staff ran basketball leagues for children and adults in many of them.

words.d: crowded, often run-down apartment buildings in a city
a park building with a gym, showers and clubrooms
the single park agency formed in 1934 when 22 Chicago park districts merged

lessons.title: The Playground Movement
lessons.mainIdea: Reformers in the early 1900s campaigned for public playgrounds, and basketball fit the small city spaces they built.
reading: The *playground movement* was a campaign in the late 1800s and early 1900s to build public places for children to play. Its leaders said city streets were dangerous and crowded. Hull-House opened a model playground in Chicago in the 1890s. Other cities soon built their own.

In 1906 the Playground Association of America was founded. Luther Gulick, the YMCA leader who had asked for basketball, became its first president. Jane Addams was one of its leaders. The group held its first national meeting in Chicago in 1907.

Many playgrounds put up hoops on posts. Basketball fit city land because it needs only a small hard surface and one ball. Cities hired play leaders to run games and teams. Those jobs grew into the profession of public *recreation*, which means organized free-time activity.

words.d: a campaign in the late 1800s and early 1900s to build public places for children to play
organized free-time activity, often run by a city or park district

look.title: Addams on Youth and the City
look.text: Addams argued that a city that gives young people no good places to play leaves them to the streets and to commercial amusements. She urged cities to treat play as a public duty.
look.cite: Jane Addams, The Spirit of Youth and the City Streets, 1909
look.prompt: According to Addams, whose job was it to provide places to play?

check.q: Who was the first president of the Playground Association of America?
check.why: Luther Gulick, the YMCA leader, became its first president in 1906.

check.q: Why did basketball fit city playgrounds?
choices: It needs only a small hard surface and one ball.
It needs a large grass field.
It was required by state law.
check.why: A small paved space and one ball were enough, which suited crowded city land.

check.q: What does recreation mean?
check.why: Recreation is organized free-time activity, a profession that grew from playground work.

lessons.title: Ballroom Teams in Philadelphia and Harlem
lessons.mainIdea: Early pro teams like the SPHAs and the Rens grew out of neighborhood clubs and played in ballrooms.
reading: Many early professional teams grew out of neighborhood clubs. In Philadelphia, a team from the South Philadelphia Hebrew Association formed in 1918. Fans called it the SPHAs. Eddie Gottlieb helped run it for decades. The team played in hotel *ballrooms*, and a dance often followed the game.

In New York, Robert Douglas founded the Renaissance Big Five in 1923. The team took its name from the Renaissance Casino and Ballroom in Harlem, where it played home games. People called the team the Rens. It was an all-Black professional team owned by a Black man.

Most white professional leagues would not admit the Rens. So the team went *barnstorming*, traveling from town to town to play any team that would schedule a game. In 1939 the Rens won the first World Professional Basketball Tournament, held in Chicago. In 1963 the whole team was elected to the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame.

words.d: large halls built for dancing, often rented for basketball games
traveling from town to town to play local teams

check.why: Robert Douglas founded the Rens and named them for the Renaissance Ballroom in Harlem.

choices: Most white pro leagues would not admit them.
check.why: Shut out of white leagues, the Rens traveled to play any team that would schedule them.

check.q: Where was the first World Professional Basketball Tournament held in 1939?
check.why: The tournament was held in Chicago, and the Rens won the first one.

lessons.title: The Globetrotters Start in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: The Harlem Globetrotters began on Chicago's South Side in the late 1920s and became a winning road team.
reading: The Harlem Globetrotters did not begin in Harlem. They began on Chicago's South Side in the late 1920s. The Savoy Ballroom opened on South Parkway in 1927, and a team of young Black players from the neighborhood played there. Abe Saperstein, a Chicago *promoter*, took a team from that circle on the road.

Saperstein chose the name Harlem because the New York neighborhood was famous as a center of Black culture. For years the team toured small towns across the Midwest. It played local teams in school gyms, halls and armories. Travel was hard, and many hotels and restaurants refused to serve Black players.

In 1940 the Globetrotters won the World Professional Basketball Tournament in Chicago. In February 1948 they beat the Minneapolis Lakers, one of the best professional teams, at Chicago Stadium. Later the Globetrotters became famous mostly for comedy *exhibitions*, shows played for entertainment rather than standings. Their early years were serious, competitive road basketball.

words.d: a person who organizes games and sells them to the public
games played for show or entertainment, not for league standings

look.title: A Name From Another City
look.text: A team formed on Chicago's South Side takes the name of a neighborhood in New York City. It plays almost all its early games in small Midwestern towns, far from both places. Posters in each town announce the Harlem Globetrotters.
look.prompt: Why might a promoter pick a name from another city? What did the name tell audiences?

check.why: The team grew out of South Side Chicago and the Savoy Ballroom circle.

check.why: The Globetrotters beat the Minneapolis Lakers, a top pro team, in 1948.

lessons.title: Factory Teams and the NBL
lessons.mainIdea: Midwest companies sponsored teams that formed the National Basketball League in 1937, and it later merged into the NBA.
reading: In the Midwest, companies paid for basketball teams. A *sponsor* pays for a team, often to advertise its name. Tire makers in Akron, Ohio, backed teams named for Firestone and Goodyear. In Fort Wayne, Indiana, Fred Zollner's piston company backed the Zollner Pistons.

In 1937 several company and town teams formed the *National Basketball League*, or NBL. Its teams were mostly in small and middle-sized cities in Ohio, Indiana, Wisconsin, Michigan and Illinois. Games were played in high school gyms, armories and local arenas. Some players also worked for the sponsoring company.

The Chicago American Gears joined the NBL and won its title in 1947. Their star was George Mikan, who had played college basketball at DePaul University in Chicago. In 1949 the NBL joined the Basketball Association of America in a *merger*. The combined league took the name National Basketball Association, or NBA.

words.d: a company or person who pays for a team, often to advertise
a pro league formed in 1937 by mostly Midwestern company and town teams
the joining of two organizations into one

check.why: The American Gears, led by George Mikan, won the 1947 NBL title.

choices: The NBL and the BAA merged to form the NBA.

lessons.title: The Illinois State Tournament
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA boys basketball tournament began in 1908 and became one of the biggest events in Illinois.
reading: The Illinois high school association held its first boys basketball *state tournament* in 1908. Peoria High School won it. For decades every school in the state, large or small, played in one bracket. In 1972 the IHSA split the tournament into two *classes*, groups of schools sorted by size.

For many years the finals were held at the University of Illinois in Champaign. Fans from small towns and big cities filled the gym. In 1939 H. V. Porter, an IHSA official, used the words March Madness in writing about the tournament. The IHSA later registered the phrase as a *trademark*, a name protected by law.

In 1954 DuSable High School of Chicago reached the state championship game. It was the first all-Black team to play for the Illinois title. DuSable lost to Mount Vernon. Girls basketball joined the IHSA state series in the 1970s, after the Title IX law opened school sports to girls.

words.d: a statewide contest in which school teams play until one champion is left
groups of schools sorted by size so similar schools play each other
a name or symbol protected by law for one owner's use

lessons.title: Basketball on the Air
lessons.mainIdea: Before television, most fans followed basketball in person, on radio or in print; the first televised game came in 1940.
reading: Before television, most fans followed basketball in person, on radio or in the newspaper. College games drew big city crowds. In 1934 promoter Ned Irish began staging college *doubleheaders* at Madison Square Garden in New York. A doubleheader is two games in the same place on the same day or night.

On February 28, 1940, an experimental station in New York *televised* a college doubleheader from Madison Square Garden. Pittsburgh played Fordham in the first game. It is usually named as the first basketball game shown on television. Only a small number of homes had TV sets then, so few people saw it.

Chicago's pro teams came and went. The Chicago Stags played in the Basketball Association of America from 1946 to 1950. The Chicago Packers began in 1961 and moved to Baltimore in 1963. The Chicago Bulls began play in 1966 and have stayed. By then television was bringing more games into homes, and the neighborhood gym had a new rival.

words.d: pairs of games played in the same place on the same day or night
shown on television
